source: Fiddick (2003) Is there a faculty of deontic reasoning? A critical re-evaluation of abstract deontic versions of the Wason selection task
finding: On the standard abstract Wason task fewer than 10 percent solve it. Early thematic versions seemed to help (Johnson-Laird 1972; Wason and Shapiro 1971) but later ones failed to replicate (Manktelow and Evans 1979). Griggs and Cox (1982) blamed prior experience, later ruled out by Cosmides (1989). This confusing pattern is what the content-effect theories were built to explain.
numbers: Standard task: under 10 percent correct (P and not-Q). No N given for these older studies.
limits: Secondary account of older studies. Numbers are not from the original papers.
agent_relevance: Content effects are not a general 'realism helps' rule. Only some contents help, so S1 must not assume that adding realistic content fixes reasoning.

source: Fiddick (2003) Is there a faculty of deontic reasoning? A critical re-evaluation of abstract deontic versions of the Wason selection task
finding: Social Contract Theory (Cosmides 1985, 1989): an evolved 'look for cheaters' algorithm fires for rules of the form 'if you take the benefit then you must pay the cost'. A cheater takes the benefit and does not pay. It makes people pick the benefit card (P) and the not-paid card (not-Q), which happens to be the logically correct pair.
numbers: Replications named by Fiddick: Cosmides and Tooby 1992; Gigerenzer and Hug 1992; Platt and Griggs 1993 (no numbers given here).
limits: Fiddick is a defender of the theory. He stresses it is narrow (social exchange), not a theory of reasoning in general. The claim that robust effects appear only for standard social contracts was a summary of past literature, not a prediction.
agent_relevance: The correct answer rides on a content cue (who could cheat). The scaffold cannot count on that cue. It should restate the rule as 'what counts as a violation' before choosing tests.

source: Fiddick (2003) Is there a faculty of deontic reasoning? A critical re-evaluation of abstract deontic versions of the Wason selection task
finding: Pragmatic Reasoning Schemas Theory (Cheng and Holyoak 1985): people hold abstract, goal-linked schemas built from experience with permissions and obligations. The permission schema has four production rules: P1 if action taken then precondition must be satisfied; P2 if action not taken then precondition need not be satisfied; P3 if precondition satisfied then action may be taken; P4 if precondition not satisfied then action must not be taken. P1 gives the P card and P4 gives the not-Q card.
numbers: Cheng and Holyoak (1985) Exp 2, abstract permission rule: 61 percent correct vs 19 percent on a nondeontic rule (as reported by Fiddick; original N not retrieved).
limits: Fiddick reports the effect was challenged as fragile (Jackson and Griggs 1990, wording of negatives; Noveck and O'Brien 1996, instructions). He says it holds with better designed problems (Girotto et al 1992; Kroger, Cheng and Holyoak 1993).
agent_relevance: A clean formal model: a schema is a small set of if-then rules deciding which cases can violate. A code 'violation-finder' operator could mimic P1 and P4.

source: Fiddick (2003) Is there a faculty of deontic reasoning? A critical re-evaluation of abstract deontic versions of the Wason selection task
finding: Abstract deontic rules are hard for Social Contract Theory. Fiddick ran abstract social contract, precaution, permission, obligation and matched control rules on naive subjects. Adaptive rules (social contract, precaution) did best, deontic rules sat in the middle, matched controls were lowest. This favours domain-specific rules over one general deontic schema.
numbers: Correct: precaution 50 percent, social contract 45, obligation 30, permission 20, situation control 15, action control 10. Adaptive pooled 48 vs deontic pooled 25. Social contract vs action control h=.83 (p<.01); precaution vs action h=.93 (p<.005). Permission vs control z=0.89 and obligation vs control z=1.14, both n.s. 20 subjects per group.
limits: Very small samples (20 per group, two problems each). The author is a defender of the evolutionary view.
agent_relevance: Even abstract but normative wording gives only 20 to 30 percent. A bare normative label is not enough. The agent should expect abstract rules to be hard and name the concrete violating case.

source: Fiddick (2003) Is there a faculty of deontic reasoning? A critical re-evaluation of abstract deontic versions of the Wason selection task
finding: Emotion test as a second view on rule type. 21 subjects chose which face saw the rule broken. Social contract violations went with anger, precaution violations with fear. Abstract permission and obligation rules also drew anger most, which fits the idea that people read abstract permissions as implicit social contracts.
numbers: Social contract: anger 67 percent of picks. Precaution: fear 86 percent. Abstract permission: anger 43, disgust 29. Abstract obligation: anger 48, fear 24. N=21.
limits: Author's own data, tiny N. Fiddick notes a Western cultural bias to read rights and duties as contracts could also explain it.
agent_relevance: The same logical form can be read as different content types by the reader. The agent must check how it read a rule, not only the rule text.

source: Fiddick (2003) Is there a faculty of deontic reasoning? A critical re-evaluation of abstract deontic versions of the Wason selection task
finding: Competing explanation: Relevance Theory (Sperber, Cara and Girotto 1995). Performance is good whenever the context makes the violating case P and not-Q manifest and makes finding violations worth the effort. Their Exp 4 'machine problem' made an abstract letter-number task easy: a repairman denies that the machine prints a 6 without an E.
numbers: Sperber et al Exp 4 machine problem: 57 percent correct on the abstract task (as reported by Fiddick). Removing the elements that highlight violations lowered performance.
limits: Fiddick argues the deontic effect persists when Sperber's supporting devices are removed (Fiddick, Cosmides and Tooby 2000). He says relevance theorists mostly ignored abstract deontic tasks.
agent_relevance: Strong hint: making the single falsifying case explicit (a denial or a fault story) lifts even a nondeontic test. That is cheap to write into a restate step.

source: Fiddick (2003) Is there a faculty of deontic reasoning? A critical re-evaluation of abstract deontic versions of the Wason selection task
finding: Nondeontic abstract rules can also yield P and not-Q selections. Evans and Lynch (1973): 'if P then NOT Q' abstract rules are routinely solved. Almor and Sloman (1996): 'if a large object is stored then a large container must be used' also gets high logical performance. Matching bias (Evans 1989) explains the negated-consequent case: people pick the cards named in the rule.
numbers: No percentages given in this chapter for these studies.
limits: Fiddick argues logically identical card choices do not show identical mental processes, so accuracy on the selection task is a weak test of the mechanism.
agent_relevance: Right-answer rate hides the route. Our checks must use content-swapped and negation-swapped variants, not one item.

source: von Sydow, Hagmayer, Metzner, Waldmann (2005) Cooperation detection and deontic reasoning in the Wason selection task
finding: Flexible Deontic Logic Theory: prescriptive rules (obligations, prohibitions) are checked against an 'ought table', not a truth table. The tester flexibly focuses on rule breakers (cheater detection) or rule followers (cooperator detection). Card choice follows that goal and the rule type. It predicts clear patterns for cooperator detection, which Social Contract Theory did not expect.
numbers: 80 students, 4 groups of 20 (obligation or prohibition x cheater or cooperator goal). q card chosen: obligation cheater 20 percent vs cooperator 70; prohibition cheater 80 vs cooperator 45. Not-q card: obligation cheater 70 vs cooperator 15; prohibition cheater 20 vs cooperator 55. P card chosen 75 to 100 percent in all four groups. Interaction rule type x goal: q card chi2=14.96, p<.001; not-q card chi2=16.98, p<.0001.
limits: Single conference paper, novel unfamiliar tribe rules, 20 per cell. The table text was garbled in extraction, so the row labels were matched to the text's predictions rather than read directly. The authors say Cosmides' altruist-detection null may come from scenario wording that did not map onto one card pattern.
agent_relevance: The right test depends on the goal (find violators or find followers) as well as the rule. S1 should state the goal and derive which cases can falsify.

source: von Sydow, Hagmayer, Metzner, Waldmann (2005) Cooperation detection and deontic reasoning in the Wason selection task
finding: Gigerenzer and Hug (1992) modified Social Contract Theory: perspective matters. People test only the cases through which the party they are cued to could be cheated. Social contract form alone is not enough. The paper also notes Cosmides' switched-contract finding (logic says P and not-Q, social exchange predicts not-P and Q).
numbers: Quoted description only. No numbers.
quote: the crucial issue about social contracts is the cheating option
limits: Second-hand account of Gigerenzer and Hug. Original not retrieved.
agent_relevance: Perspective cues change which cards are tested. If the agent frames a problem from the wrong side, its tests shift, so fix the perspective in S1.

source: von Sydow, Hagmayer, Metzner, Waldmann (2005) Cooperation detection and deontic reasoning in the Wason selection task
finding: Descriptive and prescriptive rules need different norms. Descriptive conditionals are tested for truth, ideally in a Bayesian way (Oaksford and Chater). Prescriptive rules are tested for violation or compliance, and cannot be falsified by counterexamples: a law is still a law if many break it.
numbers: Johnson-Laird and Wason (1970): 96 percent of participants chose a wrong pattern on the abstract task (as cited).
limits: Position claims from the authors' own theory.
agent_relevance: The is/ought split is a real fork. For an 'ought' rule hunt for violations by role. For a factual rule select by information gain.

source: Cosmides, Barrett, Tooby (2010) Adaptive specializations, social exchange, and the evolution of human intelligence
finding: Cosmides' summary of the social contract results: indicative conditionals give only 5 to 30 percent logically correct answers, but when violations correspond to cheating on a social contract, performance rises to 65 to 80 percent. Reported to hold for an unfamiliar contract (tattoo on the face for cassava root), across cultures including the Shiwiar of Ecuador, and for switched contracts.
numbers: Indicative rules 5 to 30 percent; social exchange with cheater detection 65 to 80 percent. No per-study N in the passage.
limits: Authors are the theory's proponents. They report no difference between familiar and unfamiliar contracts, but no N or effect size is given in the text read.
agent_relevance: Unfamiliarity does not remove the benefit of a clear cost-benefit structure. Structure of the problem matters more than topic familiarity.

source: Cosmides, Barrett, Tooby (2010) Adaptive specializations, social exchange, and the evolution of human intelligence
finding: Experiment 1 (benefit manipulation, N=25 per rule): the more the rule's requirement looks like a benefit to the actor, the better the cheater detection. 'Going out' rule 80 percent, 'staying home' 52, 'garbage' 44. A precautionary framing of the garbage rule gave 72 percent in a parallel study.
numbers: Going out 20/25=80 percent; staying home 13/25=52 (Z=2.09, p=.018, phi=.30); garbage 11/25=44 (Z=2.62, p=.0044, phi=.37); precautionary garbage 18/25=72 vs 44 (Z=2.01, p=.02). Monotonic contrast Z=3.06, p=.0011.
limits: 25 per cell; effect sizes small to medium; contrasts designed by the theory's authors.
agent_relevance: Same logic, different payoff framing: 44 to 80 percent. This measures how far content alone moves accuracy, a bar for our content-swapped test.

source: Cosmides, Barrett, Tooby (2010) Adaptive specializations, social exchange, and the evolution of human intelligence
finding: Experiment 2 (Sears problems, N=25 per rule): social contract 72 percent correct vs 48 and 32 for versions that do not look like an exchange. Experiment 3 (intention): cheater 68 percent, sabotage 45, innocent mistake 27. Experiment 4 (benefit, intention, ability, 2x2x2): full cheater condition 64 percent, falling to 26 with factors removed.
numbers: Sears: 18/25=72, signed forms 12/25=48 (Z=1.73, p=.04), filed forms 8/25=32. Exp 3: 23/34=68, 15/33=45 (p=.033), 9/33=27 (p=.0005). Exp 4: benefit F(1,342)=7.30 p=.007; intention F=10.22 p=.002; ability F=4.87 p=.028; each removed factor cost about 20 points; no interactions.
limits: Authors read the intention effect as support for cheater-specific detection. Utility and relevance accounts predict accidental violations should matter equally. Authors reply that relevance would make the benefit-plus-intention case best, which it was not.
agent_relevance: Detection is not 'any violation'. It is intentional violations that benefit the violator. A verifier should classify the failure type before acting.

source: Cosmides, Barrett, Tooby (2010) Adaptive specializations, social exchange, and the evolution of human intelligence
finding: Precautions are a second domain: 'if you engage in a hazardous activity then you must take protection'. Violations are detected well even when accidental. The authors argue this is a separate system from social exchange, with neuroimaging and brain-damage evidence (Stone et al; Fiddick et al).
numbers: Accidental precaution violations still detected (Fiddick 2004), unlike accidental social-contract violations. No percentages in the passage.
limits: Cheng and Holyoak argue precautions and social contracts share one permission schema. The Cosmides camp says that predicts equal performance across permission rules, which their Exps 1 and 2 contradict.
agent_relevance: Two rival theories agree that more than one rule type exists. Keep a short list of rule types (exchange, precaution, descriptive) and route each to its own check.

source: Cosmides, Barrett, Tooby (2010) Adaptive specializations, social exchange, and the evolution of human intelligence
finding: Authors' rebuttals to rival accounts: permission schema theory predicts equal results across permission rules (contradicted by Exps 1 and 2); general deontic logic fails because deontic rules that do not expose cheaters give poor performance; relevance theory fails because the benefit-plus-intention condition should be most relevant yet scored lower than the full condition; the material-conditional account cannot explain variation with the rule held constant.
numbers: Refers to the Experiment 4 pattern above.
limits: Author-side assessment. Fiddick (2003) and von Sydow (2005) accept part and dispute part.
agent_relevance: The field has no single winning account. A scaffold built on one theory would be a guess, so keep it theory-light.

source: Oaksford and Chater (2003) Optimal data selection: Revision, review, and reevaluation
finding: Information gain model (Oaksford and Chater 1994): in the indicative task people pick cards by expected information gain about 'rule holds' vs 'no dependency', under a rarity assumption (p and q are rare). It explains why p and q cards are chosen far more than not-q. The usual 'error' is then a sensible Bayesian answer, not a failure of logic.
numbers: Fitted to 34 meta-analysis studies; per-study fit mean G2(2)=2.60 (SD 2.55), p>.20. Not rejected in any of 28 conditions of Oaksford et al 1999, mean G2(2)=3.15 (SD 2.31). Mental logic and mental models rejected in pooled test, G2(68)=110.99.
limits: Authors defend their own model. Critics (Oberauer et al 1999; Laming 1996; Evans and Over 1996) dispute it. Authors say deontic rules need a separate expected-utility account, not information gain.
agent_relevance: A computational model of the descriptive side: choose the test with the largest expected information gain. This is computable in code and fits G5 (code selects).

source: Oaksford and Chater (2003) Optimal data selection: Revision, review, and reevaluation
finding: Observed card-selection rates in the abstract task (Table A1 of the paper), as P(select) for p, not-p, q, not-q. Wason (1968): .. p 1.00, not-p .17, q .78, not-q .28. Evans and Lynch (1973) control: p 1.00, not-p .06, q .69, not-q .12. The table also lists two Cosmides (1989) rows (Exps 1 and 2: .96 .21 .31 .44; Exps 3 and 4: .96 .23 .48 .52).
numbers: Wason (1968) not-q chosen 28 percent; Evans and Lynch (1973) control not-q 12 percent.
limits: Column order is inferred from the table header (bars lost in text extraction). Which Cosmides conditions those two rows represent is not stated in the text read, so treat the Cosmides row as indicative only.
agent_relevance: Base rates: not-q is picked 12 to 50 percent even in better groups. Use as a baseline when testing whether content-neutral rewriting helps.

source: Oaksford and Chater (2003) Optimal data selection: Revision, review, and reevaluation
finding: Dual-process positioning: Stanovich and West (1998) suggest at most about 10 percent of university students use System 2 on the selection task. Oaksford and Chater argue most reasoning is System 1 and probabilistic. About 70 percent of Green and Over (1997) participants wanted to inspect all four classes of patients, with more p and q, which no logic-only account predicts.
numbers: About 10 percent System 2 (Stanovich and West 1998, as cited). Green and Over (1997): around 70 percent. Legrenzi (1971): 1 of 30 participants described the four-card display with a conditional.
limits: Interpretation depends on the authors' probabilistic view.
agent_relevance: If logically correct selection is rare even in people, 'what people do' is a poor target. Check our agent against logic by code, not against a human norm.

source: Oaksford and Chater (2003) Optimal data selection: Revision, review, and reevaluation
finding: Dispute over probability effects: Oberauer et al (1999) ran three experiments that, they argued, failed to replicate the predicted probability effects. Oaksford and Chater reply that cues and manipulations differed. Realistic content (Oaksford et al 1999 Exps 1 and 2) did not give clean results because it cued prior knowledge, while abstract content (Exps 3 and 4) matched the predictions.
numbers: Oaksford et al 1999: with 4 high-effects conditions removed, overall G2(48)=65.45, p>.02. Not-q never exceeded q in Exp 1 with real-world content.
limits: The dispute is unresolved in the paper. It shows a content confound: realistic materials bring priors that override the manipulation.
agent_relevance: Real content brings its own priors. An evaluation set with real content needs an abstract or nonsense twin.

source: Lampinen, Dasgupta, Chan, et al. (2024) Language models show human-like content effects on reasoning tasks
finding: Language models show human-like content effects on three tasks: natural language inference (NLI), syllogism validity and the Wason selection task. Models (Chinchilla, PaLM 2-M, PaLM 2-L, Flan-PaLM 2, GPT-3.5-turbo-instruct) answer more accurately when the content supports the logical answer. Effects are small on NLI, strong on syllogisms and large on Wason.
numbers: Human N: 625 participants first, then 360 more after low Wason accuracy. NLI: no significant content effect in humans or any model (all z<1.21, p>.2). Syllogisms: significant content advantage in humans and all models (z>=2.25 or chi2>=6.39, p<=.01). Wason: realistic advantage significant for humans, Chinchilla, PaLM 2-L, GPT-3.5 (z>2.2, p<.03); marginal for PaLM 2-M and Flan-PaLM 2 (z<=1.78, p>=.08).
limits: Humans did not beat chance on Wason overall (forced two-card choice, online sample). Per-condition accuracy bars are in figures not in the text. Models are older than current frontier models.
agent_relevance: The content effect is not a small-model bug. It is a general trait of models trained on human text. The scaffold needs a content-independent check.

source: Lampinen, Dasgupta, Chan, et al. (2024) Language models show human-like content effects on reasoning tasks
finding: Item-level agreement between humans and models: items humans got right are the items models got right, even after controlling for condition. Model confidence (log-probability gap between the top two answers) is higher on correct answers, lower when the conclusion violates beliefs, and higher on realistic Wason rules.
numbers: Item-level human-model accuracy link: NLI t(832)=3.49, p<.001; syllogisms t(345)=4.98, p<.001. Confidence vs human response time: NLI t(655)=-3.39, p<.001; syllogisms t(353)=-2.03, p<.05.
limits: Correlational. Confidence uses prior-corrected log-probabilities, not the answer text.
agent_relevance: Log-prob gaps can serve as a doubt signal (fits G1), but part of the signal is content-driven, so low confidence on an unbelievable-but-valid item is not evidence of error.

source: Lampinen, Dasgupta, Chan, et al. (2024) Language models show human-like content effects on reasoning tasks
finding: Slow human responders show the realistic-content advantage on Wason; fast ones do not. The slowest 15 percent (over 80 seconds) were above chance on realistic rules and near chance on arbitrary ones. Human accuracy rose with response time. In models, instruction tuning (Flan-PaLM 2, GPT-3.5-instruct) made no consistent difference to content effects.
numbers: Slow group = top 15 percent of response times, over 80 s. Accuracy vs response time z=4.44, p<.001.
limits: The slow group is picked after the fact by time (selection effect).
agent_relevance: More time helped people only when content supported the logic. Extra thinking alone does not remove content bias (fits G11).

source: Lampinen, Dasgupta, Chan, et al. (2024) Language models show human-like content effects on reasoning tasks
finding: Prompts and few-shot examples reduce but do not remove content effects. Five examples gave mild accuracy gains. On syllogisms the content effect weakened slightly but stayed robust. On Wason with 5 shots the content effect grew because the model improved more on realistic rules. A few examples took Chinchilla on NLI from content-biased to near ceiling.
numbers: Chinchilla only, 5-shot. With prior-corrected scoring PaLM-2 L exceeded 75 percent in every Wason condition including arbitrary and nonsense; every above-chance model still did better on realistic than arbitrary rules.
limits: Few-shot tests were limited to Chinchilla for compute reasons. The scoring method (raw vs corrected log-prob) changes absolute accuracy and sometimes the pattern.
agent_relevance: Examples help on easy tasks, not on content bias on hard ones. Test any 'be logical' instruction before trusting it (our open question 2b).

source: Lampinen, Dasgupta, Chan, et al. (2024) Language models show human-like content effects on reasoning tasks
finding: The authors argue that one transformer can show dual-system behaviour: biased in some contexts and consistent in others, depending on prompt and difficulty. They suggest a separate symbolic system may not be needed and that a context-dependent control mechanism may be learned.
numbers: Qualitative argument. NLI few-shot moved Chinchilla from highly biased to near ceiling, and a simple instruction prompt reduced bias substantially.
limits: Speculative reading of the data. The authors note human control networks sit outside language areas, so the human parallel is incomplete.
agent_relevance: Supports adding control by scaffold and prompt rather than training. G1 still says apply it only on a signal.

source: Bertolazzi, Gatt, Bernardi (2024) A systematic analysis of large language models as soft reasoners: the case of syllogistic inferences
finding: With zero-shot chain-of-thought, LLaMA-2, LLaMA-3 and Pythia models mostly lose accuracy on valid syllogisms when the conclusion is unbelievable. Supervised fine-tuning removes most of the content effect and in-context learning does not. Models are weak on invalid inferences and on saying 'nothing follows'.
numbers: Humans: 44.63 percent on valid and 40.97 on invalid syllogisms (Khemlani and Johnson-Laird 2012). Valid syllogisms, believable to unbelievable: LLaMA-3 8B 70.74 to 52.59; LLaMA-2-inst 7B 32.22 to 19.26; LLaMA-3 70B-inst 54.44 to 57.41 (no loss). Spearman with human accuracy up to .87 (LLaMA-3 70B-inst).
limits: Open models only; 270 items per believable set. The percentage column in the table was not checked for its exact definition.
agent_relevance: Training on form can fix content bias, but we do not train. A content-swapped twin test is the code-side stand-in.

source: Valentino et al. (2026) Mitigating content effects on reasoning in language models through fine-grained activation steering
finding: Content effects can be shifted by steering internal activations. The authors built about 16,000 syllogisms crossing validity with plausibility, located the validity and plausibility signals in later layers, and showed a conditional steering variant (K-CAST) helps models that static steering cannot.
numbers: About 16,000 arguments; 2,400-example test set. Llama 3.2 1b zero-shot accuracy 58.17 to 73.56 with steering. K-CAST gives up to 15 points absolute gain. Static steering was ineffective on Llama 3.2 3b and Qwen 2.5 3b. In-context learning did not fix content effects and often cut accuracy.
limits: Open small models only (1b to 9b). Needs access to activations, so it cannot be used with a hosted API model.
agent_relevance: Not usable by a prompt-only scaffold, but it confirms validity and plausibility are separable directions, which supports the content-swap idea.

source: Bertolazzi, Pezzelle, Bernardi (2026) How language models conflate logical validity with plausibility: a representational analysis of content effects
finding: In LLMs, validity and plausibility are both linearly represented and strongly aligned, so the model conflates them. Adding a plausibility vector can flip a validity judgement and the reverse. The more aligned the two directions, the larger the behavioural content effect. Zero-shot prompts give larger content effects than chain-of-thought at the same alignment.
numbers: Cosine similarity between validity and plausibility vectors 0.48 to 0.64 (Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, Qwen3-14B) vs 0.10 to 0.13 and -0.12 to -0.17 for two control concepts. Reported zero-shot accuracies 80.61 percent (Qwen3-4B) to 90.91 (Qwen3-32B); chain-of-thought above 89 percent for several models.
limits: Open models. The claim that alignment predicts content effects is a cross-model correlation (mixed-effects regression).
agent_relevance: Gives a mechanistic reason for the surface effect and a mild point for chain-of-thought narrowing it. Not a guarantee.

source: Abe, Ozeki, Ando, Morishita, Mineshima, Okada (2026) Evaluation of deontic conditional reasoning in large language models: the case of Wason's selection task
finding: Modern LLMs show the deontic advantage on the Wason task: accuracy is higher on deontic than on descriptive rules for every model and prompt type, by 5.0 to 41.2 points. Error patterns fit matching bias (choosing cards named in the rule and ignoring negation) better than confirmation bias.
numbers: Accuracy on deontic rules, zero-shot (gain over descriptive): gpt-oss-20b 67.5 (+27.5); gpt-oss-120b 100.0 (+30); qwen3-14b 97.5 (+45); qwen3-32b 98.8 (+38.8); gemma3-4b 17.5 (+5); gemma3-27b 77.5 (+38.7); llama-3.3-70b 62.5 (+10); olmo-2-32b 36.2 (+15). Percentages imply about 80 trials per cell.
limits: Open-weight models only. Exact-match scoring over multi-select. One dataset, built on NeuBAROCO. Trial count inferred, not stated in the text read.
agent_relevance: Even strong reasoning models do worse on descriptive than on deontic rules, so a descriptive-rule test step should add an explicit falsifier search built by code.

source: Wikipedia: Wason selection task
finding: The entry says that in Wason's original study 'not even 10%' found the correct solution, that this was replicated by Evans, Newstead and Byrne (1993), and that most people have no trouble with the alcohol-and-age version. It cites Sperber and Girotto (2002) for the claim that the logic of testing depends on one's goals.
numbers: Under 10 percent correct (Wason 1977, as cited). Kaufman et al. (2011): 112 subjects on a 70-item contextualised Wason task.
limits: Tertiary source used only to confirm the headline baseline. It gives no numbers for drinking-age, Cosmides or Cheng and Holyoak.
agent_relevance: Baseline anchor only.

source: Cosmides (1989) The logic of social exchange: Has natural selection shaped how humans reason? Studies with the Wason selection task
finding: Founding paper of Social Contract Theory. Not opened this session (PDF URLs returned 404 or HTML pages). Used only as described by Fiddick (2003), Cosmides et al. (2010) and von Sydow et al. (2005).
numbers: Original numbers not retrieved. Secondary: social exchange 65 to 80 percent correct vs 5 to 30 percent indicative (Cosmides et al. 2010).
limits: Second-hand. Treat figures as unverified against the primary text.
agent_relevance: Open next pass: exact percentages and N for Exps 1 to 6 and the switched-contract result.

source: Cheng and Holyoak (1985) Pragmatic reasoning schemas
finding: Original pragmatic reasoning schema paper. Not opened this session. Described via Fiddick (2003): abstract permission rule 61 percent correct vs 19 percent for a nondeontic rule (Exp 2).
numbers: 61 vs 19 percent (as reported by Fiddick 2003; original N not retrieved).
limits: Not read. The familiarity comparison between two student groups in the original was not verified here.
agent_relevance: Open next pass.

source: Sperber, Cara and Girotto (1995) Relevance theory explains the selection task
finding: Original relevance-theory account of the selection task. Not opened (PDF host unavailable). Described by Fiddick (2003) and Oaksford and Chater (2003): the machine problem gave 57 percent correct on an abstract task, and removing violation-highlighting elements lowered it.
numbers: 57 percent (Exp 4 machine problem, as reported by Fiddick 2003).
limits: Not read. Oaksford and Chater (2003) argue the effects manipulation is better explained by decision-theoretic accounts.
agent_relevance: Open next pass for the cognitive-effect model.
